overview.summary: Set designers design the physical surroundings for theatre, film, television and events, creating the places where stories happen.
overview.problems: They turn a script and the director's vision into rooms, streets and worlds that look right and work for the actors and the camera.
overview.worksWith: Directors, producers, art directors, builders, prop and costume teams, lighting designers and actors.
overview.workplaces: Theatres, film and TV studios, workshops and location sites, and design offices.

timeline.title: Read and research
timeline.description: The designer reads the script and researches the period, place and mood.
timeline.why: The set must support the story.

timeline.title: Sketching and model making
timeline.description: The designer draws plans and builds small scale models to test ideas.
timeline.why: Small models show problems before big builds.

timeline.title: Meeting the director and team
timeline.description: The designer presents ideas and adjusts to feedback.
timeline.why: The set must work for the whole production.

timeline.title: Planning construction
timeline.description: The designer draws technical plans, chooses materials and calculates costs for the builders.
timeline.why: Designs must be buildable and affordable.

timeline.title: Visiting the workshop or set
timeline.description: The designer checks progress and solves problems with carpenters and painters.
timeline.why: Ideas often need adjusting while they are built.

timeline.title: Tight deadlines
timeline.description: Sets must be ready before shooting or opening night.

responsibilities: Making sure sets are safe for performers and crew
challenges: Work is project-based and income can be uneven.
Days are long when a production is close to opening.
Competition for jobs is strong, and portfolios and connections matter.
Sets often exist only for a short time.
Workshops and sets involve physical work and some risks.
Many people's needs have to be balanced.
workEnvironment: Design offices, workshops, theatres and film sets, often with long days near production deadlines. Work moves between drawing, meetings and practical building. Many set designers work freelance.
rewards: A mix of art, craft and practical work
Seeing your design on stage or screen
tradeoffs: Pay that varies by country and sector

activity.title: Build a shoebox model of a scene
steps: Choose a scene from a story or write a short one, such as a kitchen at night.
Sketch how the room should look and what the audience needs to see.
Build it inside a shoebox with paper, card and fabric scraps.
Light it with a torch to see how the mood changes.
Ask someone what story it tells and revise.
activity.outcome: You practise turning a story into a space and testing the mood.
activity.safety: Use only paper, card and a torch, ask an adult for help with scissors, and avoid candles, hot glue or anything that heats.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
